candidate.derivedAnswer: D. Two rays, including the foci, under the recorded distinct-focus convention.
candidate.answerReason: For distinct foci, triangle-side inequalities exclude noncollinear points, and segment addition excludes points strictly between the foci. Equality holds on both outward rays, including their starting foci. If coincident foci were allowed, the locus would be the whole plane.

methods.label: Triangle-side inequalities and segment addition
methods.explanation:
Assume the foci \(F_1,F_2\) are distinct, as recorded, and let \(d=F_1F_2>0\). The condition is \(|PF_1-PF_2|=d\). Comparing the three distances helps determine where \(P\) can lie.

If \(P\) is not on the line through the foci, the triangle-side inequality gives \(|PF_1-PF_2|<d\), excluding such points. If \(P\) lies strictly between the foci, both focal distances are positive and their sum is \(d\), so their absolute difference is also less than \(d\).

On either outward extension of the focal segment, the longer focal distance equals the shorter distance plus \(d\), so the required equality holds. It also holds at each focus. Thus the locus is two outward rays, each including its starting focus: choice D.

The distinct-focus condition matters: if the foci coincided, every point would satisfy \(0=0\), giving the whole plane.
